entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen27795" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27796" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27796" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27798" type="x-p"/> Prophecy of great prosperity under Hezekiah; but, in its highest sense, applicable to Christ, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.8">Isa 32:1-8</reference>. Description of impending calamities, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:9-14</reference>. Rejection of the Jews, and calling of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Isa 32:15</reference>. The future prosperity of the Church, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.16-Isa.32.20">Isa 32:16-20</reference>. <div eID="gen27798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27799" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27800" type="x-p"/> Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness - If King Hezekiah were a type of Christ, then this prophecy may refer to his time; but otherwise it seems to have Hezekiah primarily in view. It is evident, however, that in the fullest sense these words cannot be applied to any man; God alone can do all that is promised here. <div eID="gen27800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27801" type="x-p"/> And princes - ושרים ve-sarim, without ל lamed, to; so the ancient Versions. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27809" type="x-p"/> And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim "And him the eyes of those that see shall regard" - For ולא velo, and not, Le Clerc reads ולו velo, and to him, of which mistake the Masoretes acknowledge there are fifteen instances; and many more are reckoned by others. The removal of the negative restores to the verb its true and usual sense.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27820" type="x-p"/> The vile person will speak villany "The fool will still utter folly" - A sort of proverbial saying, which Euripides (Bacchae, 369) has expressed in the very same manner and words: Μωρα γαρ μωρος λεγει· "The fool speaks folly. "Of this kind of simple and unadorned proverb or parable, see De S. Poes, Hebr. Praelect. xxiv. <div eID="gen27820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27821" type="x-p"/> Against the Lord "Against Jehovah" - For אל El, two MSS. read אל al, more properly; but both are of nearly the same meaning.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27822" type="x-p"/> The instruments also of the churl are evil "As for the niggard, his instruments are evil" - His machinations, his designs. The paronomasia, which the prophet frequently deals in, suggested this expression וכלי כליו vechelai kelaiv. The first word is expressed with some variety in the MSS. Seven MSS. read וכילי vekili, one וכל vechol, another וכולי vecoli. <div eID="gen27822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27823" type="x-p"/> To destroy the poor with lying words "To defeat the assertions of the poor in judgment" - A word seems to have been lost here, and two others to have suffered a small alteration, which has made the sentence very obscure. The Septuagint have happily retained the rendering of the lost word, and restored the sentence in all its parts: Και διασκεδασαι λογους ταπεινων εν κρισει· ולהפר דברי אביון במשפט ulehapher dibrey ebyon bemishpat, "And disperse the words of the poor in judgment. "They frequently render the verb הפר haphar by διασκεδασαι, A MS. reads ולדבר uledabber, which gives authority for the preposition ל lamed, to, necessary to the sense, and the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee read במשפט bemishpat, In judgment.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27824" type="x-p"/> Liberal things "Generous purposes" - "Of the four sorts of persons mentioned <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Isa 32:5</reference>, three are described, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.7">Isa 32:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa 32:8</reference>, but not the fourth." - Secker. Perhaps for והוא vehu, and he, we ought to read ושוע veshoa, the bountiful.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27829" type="x-p"/> They shall lament - for the pleasant fields "Mourn ye for the pleasant field" - The Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate read ספדו siphdu, mourn ye, imperative; twelve MSS., (five ancient), two editions, the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Syriac, and Vulgate, all read שדה sadeh, a field; not שדי shedey, breasts.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27830" type="x-p"/> Shall come up thorns and briers "The thorn and the brier shall come up" - All the ancient Versions read ושמיר veshamir, with the conjunction. And an ancient MS. has תעלה בו taaleh bo, "shall come up in it, "which seems to be right; or rather בה bah: and there is a rasure in the place of בו bo in another ancient MS. <div eID="gen27830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27831" type="x-p"/> Yea, upon all the houses of joy - For כי ki, the ancient Versions, except the Vulgate, seem to have read ו ve. כי ki may perhaps be a mistake for בו bo, or בה bah, in it, above mentioned. It is not necessary in this place. <div eID="gen27831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27832" type="x-p"/> The description of impending distress which begins at <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference> belongs to other times than that of Sennacherib's invasion, from which they were so soon delivered. It must at least extend to the ruin of the country and city by the Chaldeans. And the promise of blessings which follows was not fulfilled under the Mosaic dispensation; they belong to the Kingdom of Messiah. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Isa 32:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Isa 29:17</reference> (note), and see the note there.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27833" type="x-p"/> The palaces shall be forsaken - The house of the sanctuary (the temple) shall be destroyed. - Targum. <div eID="gen27833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27834" type="x-p"/> The forts "Ophel" - It was a part of Mount Zion, rising higher than the rest, at the eastern extremity, near to the temple, a little to the south of it; called by Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.8">Mic 4:8</reference>, "Ophel of the daughter of Zion. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27836" type="x-p"/> The work of righteousness - Righteousness works and produces peace. <div eID="gen27836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27837" type="x-p"/> The effect of righteousness - עבדת abodath, the culture. Righteousness, cultivated by peace, produces tranquillity of mind and permanent security. Reader, hast thou the principle? If so, dost thou cultivate it? If thou dost, thou hast peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Ghost, and a sure and certain hope of everlasting life.

Saltus; Assyriorum regnum: civitas; magnifica Assyriorum castra. Ephrem Syr. ire loc. For וברד ubarad, a MS. has וירד vaiyered; and so conjectured Abp. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen27838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27839" type="x-p"/> That sow beside all waters "Who sow your seed in every well-watered place" - Sir John Chardin's note on this place is: "This exactly answers the manner of planting rice; for they sow it upon the water, and before sowing, while the earth is covered with water, they cause the ground to be trodden by oxen, horses, and asses, who go mid-leg deep; and this is the way of preparing the ground for sowing. As they sow the rice on the water, they transplant it in the water. "Harmer's Observ. vol. 1 p. 280. "Rice is the food of two-thirds of mankind." Dr. Arbuthnot. "It is cultivated in most of the eastern countries." Miller. "It is good for all, and at all times." Sir J. Chardin, ib. "Le ris, qui est leur principal aliment et leur froment (i.e., des Siamois), n'est jamais assez arrose; il croit au milieu de l'eau, et les campagnes ou on le cultive ressemblent plutot a de marets que non pas a des terres qu'on laboure aver la charue. Le ris a bien cette force, que quoy qu'il y ait six ou sept pieds d'eau sur lui, il pousse toujours sa tige au dessus; et le tuyau qui le porte s'eleve et croit a proportion de la hauteur de l'eau qui noye son champ. Voyage de l'Eveque de Beryte, p. 144. Paris, 1666. - L. "Rice, which is the principal grain and aliment of the Siamese, can never be too much watered. It grows in the water, and the fields where it is sown resemble marshes rather than fields cultivated by ploughing. Rice has that property that although it be covered with water six or seven feet deep, yet it raises its stalk above it; and this grows long in proportion to the depth of the water by which the field is inundated."  <chapter eID="Isa.32"/> <div eID="gen27839" type="x-p"/>
